edition.name: Koetschau, Origenes Werke V: De Principiis (GCS 22, Leipzig: Hinrichs 1913) - Rufinus' Latin, with the Philocalia Greek for III.1 and IV.1-3; text from Internet Archive OCR (hOCR of scan 'origeneswerke05orig', gaps filled from second scan 'origeneswerke05orig_0')
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Videamus nune breviter quid etiam de repromissionibus sentiendum sit. Certum est quia nullum animal omnimodis otiosum atque immobile esse potest, sed omni genere moveri et agere semper et velle aliquid gestit; et hanc inesse naturam omnibus animantibus manifestum puto. Multo ergo magis rationabile animal, id est hominis naturam necesse est semper aliquid movere vel agere. Et si quidem immemor sui sit eb quid se deceat ignoret, circa usus corporales omnis sua movetur intentio et per omnes motus suos erga voluptates ac libidines corporis oecupatur; si vero talis sit, qui in commune aliquid curare vel providere studeat, aut rei publicae consulens aut magistratibus parens aut quidquid illud est, quod in commune certe prodesse videatur, exercet. Jam vero si qui talis sit, ut aliquid melius quam haee, quae corporea videntur, intellegat et sapientiae ac scientiae operam navet, sine dubio erga huiuscemodi studia omnem sui declinabit industriam, quo possit inquisita veritate rerum causas rationemque cognoscere. Nicut ergo in hae vita alius quidem summum bonum corporis iudicat voluptatem, alius vero in commune consulere, alius studus et intellegentiae operam dare: ita requirimus in illa “vitae quae vera est, quae “abscondita essedicitur -cum Christo in deo’, id est in illa aeterna vita, si aliqui talis erii nobis vivendi ordo vel status.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see now briefly what is also to be thought about the promises. It is certain because no animal at all can be idle and immobile, but it strives to be moved and to do something and to will something always and in every way; and I think it is manifest that this nature is in all living things. Therefore much more the rational animal, that is the nature of man, it is necessary always to move or to do something. And if indeed he is forgetful of himself and ignores what is fitting for him, his entire intention is moved around bodily uses and through all his movements he is occupied with the pleasures and desires of the body; if however he is such a one who strives to care for or provide something in common, either consulting for the republic or obeying the magistrates or whatever that is which certainly seems to be of use in common, he exercises. Now indeed if someone is such that he understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, without doubt he will direct all his industry towards such studies, so that he may know the causes and reason of things investigated. Just as therefore in this life one judges the greatest good of the body to be pleasure, another to consult for the common good, another to devote himself to studies and intelligence: so we require in that life which is true, which is called hidden with Christ in God, that is in that eternal life, if such a one will be for us a way of living or a status.
pass_b_english: Let us now briefly consider what we should think about the promises as well. It is certain that no animal at all can be entirely idle and immobile; rather, it strives to be moved and to act in every way, always willing to do something. I think it is clear that this nature belongs to all living things. Therefore, the rational animal — that is, human nature — must always be moving or doing something. If someone is forgetful of himself and ignores what befits him, his whole intention is directed toward bodily uses, and through all his movements he is occupied with the body's pleasures and desires. If, however, he is the sort who strives to care for or provide something in common — whether advising for the republic, supporting the magistrates, or exercising whatever certainly seems to benefit the common good — he pursues that. Now, if someone is such that he understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, without doubt he will direct all his industry toward such studies, so that he may come to know the causes and reason of things investigated. Just as, then, in this life one person judges the body's greatest good to be pleasure, another strives to consult for the common good, and another devotes himself to studies and intelligence: so we ask that in that true life, which is called "hidden with Christ in God" — that is, in that eternal life — such a way of living or state might exist for us. (Colossians 3:3)

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex conditional and comparative structures. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the scripture citation (Colossians 3:3) for the phrase 'abscondita essedicitur -cum Christo in deo' (called hidden with Christ in God), which is required by the rules for added identifications.
